scenario: AITA for insisting that my son’s therapist tells me why my son wants to see him. | My son [17] was always a normal boy, with many friends, very active and didn’t seam to have any kind of problem. But one day we he told us he needed to go see a therapist. We were really surprised by that, we never thought he will ask us something like that. We ask him why but he didn’t want to tell us. We were worried so we send him to a therapist and now he goes once a week. In our eyes he is still the same kid that before. We tried to think about things that he may have. We thought maybe he is bulimic or anorexic ( as he is very thin ) but he isn’t that skinny and those things tend to affect women, not men. We thought of depression but that also doesn’t seem very likely. We decided that theorizing wouldn’t give us an answer so we ask his therapist and refused, saying that he couldn’t say what my son told him. I told him that we didn’t want the specifics but at least the reason why he goes to therapy. But he refused again. We try to insist many times but he didn’t give up. And the day after, our son come to us and tell us that he know that we insisted on knowing why he wants therapy ( we don’t know if the therapist told him or maybe he hear us talking about it in the house ) and insulted us. He didn’t talk to us for the rest of the day. Now, we know that insist to know wasn’t the best idea but we are his parents and we deserve to know. We really are assholes?

The parents now feel they were wrong to insist but still feel they deserve to know. So, the question is: were the parents right or wrong? I need to think about this from different angles. First, confidentiality in therapy is a big deal. Therapists are bound by laws and ethics to keep their clients' information private. Even if the client is a minor, there are limits to what can be disclosed to parents. The therapist's refusal to share details is likely due to these confidentiality rules. So, the parents insisting might be seen as overstepping, but they're also concerned about their child. On the other hand, parents have a right to know what's going on with their child, especially when it comes to their mental health. They might feel that they're not being kept in the loop, which can cause anxiety and worry. They might think that knowing the reason would help them support their son better. But by insisting, they might have made their son feel that his privacy is being invaded. The son reacted negatively, which could harm the trust between them. It's possible that the son felt pressured or judged, leading to the insult and withdrawal. I also need to consider the son's age. At 17, he's almost an adult, and he might feel that he has the right to privacy, especially regarding his mental health. The parents might have good intentions, but their approach could be seen as intrusive. Another angle is the impact on the therapeutic relationship. The son might feel that his privacy isn't respected, which could hinder his progress in therapy. So, weighing these factors, the parents' actions might be seen as wrong because they disregarded the confidentiality and privacy that their son needs, especially as he's approaching adulthood. Their intentions were good, but their method of insisting on knowing might have been the wrong approach. It's important for parents to support their children's autonomy while still being there for them when needed. I think the key here is balance. Parents should communicate their concerns without overstepping boundaries. They could have approached the situation by expressing their worries to their son directly, rather than through the therapist, respecting his privacy and need for confidentiality.
